Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-06-04", "authors": [{"authorId": "2346977046", "name": "Ke Fei"}, {"authorId": "2109058078", "name": "Jing-Jing Li"}, {"authorId": "2300955584", "name": "Xinyue Zhang"}, {"authorId": "2260379253", "name": "Kun Zheng"}, {"authorId": "2352871797", "name": "Tianxu Ji"}, {"authorId": "2158624811", "name": "Wei Wang"}, {"authorId": "2301175821", "name": "Hongkai Qi"}], "abstract": "In recommender systems, accurate post-click conversion rate (CVR) estimation is crucial for a company\u2019s revenue growth. Currently, multi-task causal methods\u2014such as multi-task doubly robust learning\u2014improve CVR estimation by reducing bias and variance during training. However, these methods often overlook the impact of hard-to-classify samples, which deviate significantly from the sample cluster center and substantially increase the bias and variance of multi-task causal approaches. To address this limitation, we propose a novel inverse contrastive representation learning guided causal multi-task framework. Specifically, we first select clicked and unclicked samples that deviate significantly from their respective cluster centers to form negative pairs. We then apply inverse contrastive representation learning (ICRL) to pull these negative pairs closer together, encouraging deviated clicked samples to move closer to the clicked cluster center, and vice versa. This approach yields a more accurate and lower-variance inverse propensity score for the CVR estimator. Additionally, we compute the ICRL loss segmentally to reduce computational resource consumption. We conduct extensive experiments on six large-scale datasets, as well as online A/B tests on our advertising platform. Our method achieves a 2.9% improvement on offline datasets compared to state-of-the-art baselines, and a 0.6% increase over the online production model."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "3f5f90fdb77857b77f7f98c524b9eff62c090590", "externalIds": {"DBLP": "journals/ijon/YuXZL26", "DOI": "10.1016/j.neucom.2026.134282", "CorpusId": 289422542}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/3f5f90fdb77857b77f7f98c524b9eff62c090590", "title": "SecFace: Secure face recognition in encrypted domain based on deep neural networks", "venue": "Neurocomputing", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1016/j.neucom.2026.134282?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2026.134282, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Kobourov"}, {"authorId": "2385516847", "name": "Jacob Miller"}], "abstract": "\n Dimensionality reduction (DR) techniques are often characterized by whether they preserve global, high\u2010level structures in the data or local, neighborhood structures. This distinction matters in visualization: global methods can obscure clusters while local methods can over\u2010emphasize them. Yet, even when clusters appear distinct, their relative arrangement in the projection may be arbitrary or misleading, a common issue in techniques such as t\u2010SNE and UMAP. Existing cluster quality metrics either only measure cluster separability or assume spherical, globular clusters in the original space. We introduce the Class Angular Distortion Index (CADI), a metric that uses internal angles among point triples to determine the faithfulness of cluster organization in a projection. We show cases on both real and synthetic data where existing cluster metrics fail, but CADI provides an interpretable result. Since it relies on computing angles, CADI is also differentiable, enabling optimization. We demonstrate this with a CADI\u2010based DR technique."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "2cadfbe27553801ac884e2c3d95765071c9f6b83", "externalIds": {"DBLP": "journals/tce/RenZZFYZ26", "DOI": "10.1109/TCE.2026.3686635", "CorpusId": 287732258}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/2cadfbe27553801ac884e2c3d95765071c9f6b83", "title": "Diff-IR: A Non-Autoregressive End-to-End Framework for Generative Image Retrieval via Diffusion Models", "venue": "IEEE transactions on consumer electronics", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1109/TCE.2026.3686635?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1109/TCE.2026.3686635, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Motivated by this progress, we propose Diff-IR, a novel generative image retrieval framework that reformulates retrieval as a non-autoregressive sequence generation task. Instead of the conventional two-stage pipeline\u2014feature extraction followed by similarity search\u2014Diff-IR directly encodes each query image into a compact discrete sequence whose code uniquely matches database images. This end-to-end design eliminates explicit similarity computation. In Diff-IR, high-level semantics are first extracted via a pre-trained CLIP encoder. The query features and a noise sequence are then processed by a Transformer-based denoising network, which gradually reconstructs the target discrete representation. Experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that treating retrieval as a generative task with diffusion not only improves accuracy but also offers efficient, fully end-to-end retrieval. Espa\u00f1ola"}], "abstract": "This technical paper presents a Teacher-Student Feature Regression (TSFR) model for anomalous sound detection utilizing the DCASE2023 Developmental Dataset, which is comprised of different machinery sounds including fan, gearbox, toycar, valve, etc. The pretrained audio neural network (PANN) CNN14 was selected as the Teacher Network to generate the latent features of the basic CNN-based Student Network. The proposed model used cosine similarity loss, mean squared error (MSE), and lambda variance for feature alignment and generalization. The model included an adjustable machine-specific hyperparameter configuration setup that allows the setting of model parameters such as masking, loss functional alpha, variance, k -pooling. The anomaly scores were based on the feature reconstruction discrepancy between the two models that are used to compute the Area-Under Receiver Operating Characteristic-Curve (AUC) and partial-AUC metrics. Experimental results show individual AUC values of $0.60,0.63,0.69,0.55,0.56,0.53$, and 0.56, generating an average of 0.59. Partial AUC metric results show values of $0.56,0.52,0.66,0.49,0.50,0.48$, and 0.51, with an average of 0.55. This indicates that the performance of the Student Network generated is comparable with the baseline autoencoder Teacher network, with AUC and pAUC values of 0.52 and 0.53 respectively. The developed model addressed the high resource and dimensionality requirement of the baseline autoencoder model using a CNNbased student network, making edge computing possible for anomalous sound detection applications."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "5848c9243250d62ca3049b85a887475af17c52f2", "externalIds": {"DBLP": "journals/corr/abs-2604-01590", "ArXiv": "2604.01590", "DOI": "10.1109/TASLPRO.2025.3642540", "CorpusId": 283868297}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/5848c9243250d62ca3049b85a887475af17c52f2", "title": "PhiNet: Speaker Verification With Phonetic Interpretability", "venue": "IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.01590", "status": "GREEN", "license": "public-domain", "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01590, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Motivated by how human experts perform forensic speaker comparison (FSC), we propose a speaker verification network with phonetic interpretability, PhiNet, designed to enhance both local and global interpretability by leveraging phonetic evidence in decision-making. For users, PhiNet provides detailed phonetic-level comparisons that enable manual inspection of speaker-specific features and facilitate a more critical evaluation of verification outcomes. For developers, it offers explicit reasoning behind verification decisions, simplifying error tracing and informing hyperparameter selection. In our experiments, we demonstrate PhiNet\u2019s interpretability with practical examples, including its application in analyzing the impact of different hyperparameters. We conduct both qualitative and quantitative evaluations of the proposed interpretability methods and assess speaker verification performance across multiple benchmark datasets, including VoxCeleb, SITW, and LibriSpeech. Bhanu"}], "abstract": "Body-based human recognition faces increased complexity due to a myriad of challenging factors such as variations in imaging platform (ground- vs. aerial-based), diverse sensors, imaging distance, changes in clothing, arbitrary human poses, occlusion and articulation of the human body, and air turbulence. These conditions often make it difficult to discern facial features, particularly at long distances, where changes in attire also significantly contribute to recognition errors. The most commonly used RGB and shape-based features extracted from color video, suffer significant drawbacks under such conditions. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces a novel biometric that integrates shape, appearance, and soft biometric features into a single, unified representation called the Outfit Regularizing Biometric (ORB). Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that the ORB representation effectively addresses some of the most significant obstacles in human recognition. We report our findings using the rigorous evaluation protocols of the BRIAR datasets (Phase 1 and 2), alongside widely used clothes-changing datasets such as PRCC, LTCC, Celeb-ReID, and VC-Clothes. Our analysis using the BRIAR dataset enables us to isolate and examine the impact of various artifacts, including changes in clothing, environmental conditions, and varying imaging distances. By employing the ORB representation, in combination with both appearance and shape-based features, and leveraging a transformer-based backbone (TransFuse), we achieve superior performance. Across different challenging scenarios, ORB consistently outperforms traditional RGB-based systems, delivering nearly an 18% improvement in accuracy on the standard BRIAR setup."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "6a62bbda5e8c22f7cbc6816622ffa14d342cab60", "externalIds": {"DOI": "10.1117/12.3096444", "CorpusId": 286085750}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/6a62bbda5e8c22f7cbc6816622ffa14d342cab60", "title": "A novel composite metric loss for offline handwritten Chinese character recognition with CNNs", "venue": "International Conference on Machine Vision", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1117/12.3096444?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1117/12.3096444, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Arlazarov"}], "abstract": "Offline handwritten Chinese character recognition remains a challenging problem in computer vision due to the large number of classes, their visual complexity, high inter-class similarity, and variability in handwriting styles. In this paper, we propose a novel composite metric loss function designed as a replacement for the widely used triplet loss in embedding-based training. The proposed loss combines three distinct components, each contributing to improved discriminative power and robustness of the learned embeddings in the feature space. To evaluate the effectiveness of the loss, we use a modified version of the lightweight HCCR-AlexNet architecture, where the final fully connected softmax layer is replaced with a low-dimensional embedding layer and train the model on the CASIA-HWDB dataset using our composite loss. Experimental results on the ICDAR-2013 test set show that the proposed loss outperforms both the triplet loss and the cross-entropy baseline in terms of top-1 accuracy. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-01-06", "authors": [{"authorId": "2403052285", "name": "Adnan Yaqoob Salik"}, {"authorId": "2298664618", "name": "Shehzad Khalid"}, {"authorId": "40988624", "name": "Ramsha Ahmed"}, {"authorId": "2403053507", "name": "Fathi Awad"}, {"authorId": "2266462235", "name": "Umer Hameed Shah"}, {"authorId": "2281871308", "name": "Taimur Hassan"}], "abstract": "Retinal diseases are considered the leading cause of blindness worldwide. Many researchers have developed autonomous retinal screening methods using optical coherence tomography (OCT), as they can reveal retinal abnormalities in the early stages. However, most of these methods lack the capability of performing retinal disease classification tasks by analyzing the disease-specific clinical manifestations, and they screen the retina by relying on mathematical features, which might not be meaningful for clinicians. To overcome these issues, we present a novel language-assisted learnable hyperdimensional computing (HDC) framework. HDC is a computational paradigm that represents and processes data using high-dimensional vector spaces to enable efficient, brain-inspired learning and reasoning. By fusing the language features and HDC visual embeddings computed through the set of clinical prompts and OCT scans, respectively, the proposed framework, with one-time training, can robustly recognize different retinal diseases irrespective of the scanner specifications, vendor artifacts, and dataset variations.
